units.title: Unit 93 — Addition and contrast
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 93. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Adding information and expressing contrast, concession and unexpected results
learningObjectives: Add information using also, as well, too, what’s more, in addition, as well as and besides.
Choose noun or -ing constructions after as well as, in addition to and besides.
Contrast although and even though + clause with despite and in spite of + noun/-ing.
Use however, yet, though and still to introduce or emphasise unexpected information.
Compare different facts using whereas and while, distinguishing contrasting from time meanings.

items.example: The apartment is bright and surprisingly quiet.
items.note: The most common coordinator for joining two related ideas or items.

items.example: The course covers speaking and also includes writing practice.
items.note: Adds more information; it typically comes before a main verb but after the verb be.

items.example: The room has a balcony and a large window as well.
items.note: Often placed at the end of the clause; similar in meaning to too.

items.example: We visited the castle and the nearby museum too.
items.note: Usually placed at the end of a clause to add a similar fact.

items.example: As well as the main course, the meal includes a dessert.
items.note: A multiword preposition followed by a noun, pronoun or -ing form, not a finite clause.

items.example: As well as studying French, he volunteers at the library.
items.note: Use an -ing form after as well as when you add another activity.

items.example: The flat is close to the station. What’s more, the rent is affordable.
items.note: Introduces an additional, often persuasive point; commonly starts a new sentence.

items.example: The hotel provides breakfast. In addition, guests can use the pool.
items.note: A sentence connector; unlike in addition to, it is not immediately followed by a noun phrase.

items.example: In addition to the rent, we have to pay for electricity.
items.note: Follow with a noun or -ing form, not a complete finite clause.

items.example: In addition to working at a school, she studies in the evenings.
items.note: Shows the -ing construction required after the preposition to in this linker.

items.example: I enjoy living here. Besides, my family is nearby.
items.note: Can add another argument at sentence level, or take a noun/-ing complement.

items.pt: além de ser; além de estar
items.example: Besides being a good designer, she is an excellent teacher.
items.note: After besides meaning in addition to, use an -ing form to introduce an activity or state.

items.example: Although we booked late, we found a good hotel.
items.note: Follow with a clause containing a subject and verb; it can introduce the first or second clause.

items.pt: embora; mesmo que; apesar de que
items.example: Even though the journey was long, everyone enjoyed it.
items.note: Emphasises an unexpected contrast more strongly than although; normally introduces a factual clause.

items.example: Despite the heavy rain, the event went ahead.
items.note: Follow directly with a noun phrase or -ing form; do not add of after despite.

items.pt: apesar de estar cansado; apesar de se sentir cansado
items.example: Despite feeling tired, she stayed until the end of the meeting.
items.note: Despite + -ing presents an unexpected result without using a full clause.

items.pt: apesar do fato de que; embora
items.example: Despite the fact that we were busy, we found time to help.
items.note: The fact that introduces a finite clause after despite; contrast with despite + noun/-ing.

items.example: In spite of the delay, we arrived before lunch.
items.note: Equivalent to despite; normally followed by a noun phrase or an -ing form.

items.pt: apesar de trabalhar; apesar de ter trabalhado
items.example: In spite of working all weekend, he did not finish the project.
items.note: Use an -ing form after the preposition of; the context determines the time reference.

items.word: in spite of the fact that
items.pt: apesar do fato de que; embora
items.example: In spite of the fact that the car was old, it ran well.
items.note: The fact that permits a finite clause after in spite of.

items.pt: mesmo assim; ainda assim; apesar disso
items.example: The instructions were difficult, but I still managed to assemble the desk.
items.note: Emphasises that the result was unexpected; distinct from still meaning continuing until now.

items.section: C · Contrast across clauses and sentences
items.example: The plan seems expensive. However, it could save time later.
items.note: A contrastive connector, often beginning a separate sentence and followed by a comma.

items.section: C · Contrast across clauses and sentences
items.example: The kitchen, however, was surprisingly spacious.
items.note: However may interrupt a clause between commas; its meaning is still contrast.

items.section: C · Contrast across clauses and sentences
items.example: The film was quite short, yet it felt very slow.
items.note: A coordinator introducing a surprising contrast, often after a comma.

items.section: C · Contrast across clauses and sentences
items.example: The room was rather small. The view was excellent, though.
items.note: In this conversational use, though often comes at the end of the clause after a comma.

items.pt: mas ainda assim; mas mesmo assim
items.section: C · Contrast across clauses and sentences
items.example: The instructions were confusing, but still, we completed the task.
items.note: Combines a common contrast conjunction with emphasis on an unexpected outcome.

items.example: I prefer quiet beaches, while my friends like busy resorts.
items.note: Here compares opposing facts; different from while meaning during the time that.

items.pt: enquanto; ao passo que; ao contrário de
items.example: Her first job was in sales, whereas her current role is in design.
items.note: Introduces a contrasting fact, often in the second clause of a sentence.

sectionsChecked: A: Adding information with as well, as well as, what’s more, in addition (to), besides, and also
B: Concession with although, even though, despite, in spite of and emphatic still
C: However in different positions, yet and final-position though
D: While and whereas used for contrasts
Exercises 93.1–93.5: connector classification, construction choices, matching and open responses

units.title: Unit 94 — Reason, purpose, result, condition
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 94. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
units.category: Linking causes, intentions, consequences and conditions
learningObjectives: Explain reasons using because + clause, as/since + clause, because of + noun and due to + noun.
Express purpose with the purpose of, so (that) + clause and (in order) to + infinitive.
Connect causes to results with so, therefore and as a result, recognising register differences.
Describe uncertainty and conditions with whether, if, unless, otherwise and as long as.
Distinguish preventive action with in case from an ordinary condition introduced by if.

items.example: We stayed indoors because the wind was very strong.
items.note: Because introduces a reason clause with a subject and verb, not just a noun phrase.

items.example: As the library was closed, I returned the next morning.
items.note: At the beginning of a sentence, as can give a reason; here it does not mean while.

items.pt: já que; visto que; uma vez que
items.example: Since you have finished early, you can leave now.
items.note: A reason connector followed by a clause; distinguish from since used for time.

items.pt: o motivo era que; a razão foi que
items.example: The reason we cancelled the picnic was that the weather changed.
items.note: Use the reason + clause + was that + clause to explain why something happened.

items.example: The outdoor concert was cancelled because of the storm.
items.note: Follow with a noun or noun phrase; do not use because of directly before a full clause.

items.example: The flight was delayed due to thick fog.
items.note: Similar to because of; often used after be and particularly to explain difficulties.

items.pt: ser devido a; ser causado por
items.example: The late delivery may be due to a transport problem.
items.note: In the causal sense, due to can follow a form of the verb be.

items.pt: o motivo de; a razão para
items.example: Nobody explained the reason for the sudden change.
items.note: A useful reason + for + noun pattern; compare the reason ... was that + clause.

items.example: The main purpose of the visit is to meet the new team.
items.note: An intention or aim: why someone is doing something.

items.pt: o objetivo é; a finalidade é
items.example: The purpose of this exercise is to improve your accuracy.
items.note: The purpose of + noun + is to + base verb states an aim.

items.pt: para que; a fim de que
items.example: I moved closer so that everyone could hear me.
items.note: Introduces a purpose clause; often followed by a subject and can, could or would.

items.example: I left early so I could avoid the traffic.
items.note: That is optional in many purpose clauses: so I could and so that I could both work.

items.example: We bought a map in order to find the correct route.
items.note: Introduces a purpose with a base-form verb; more explicit than to on its own.

items.pt: para melhorar; a fim de melhorar
items.example: She attends evening classes to improve her English.
items.note: The infinitive with to can express purpose without in order.

items.pt: para evitar; a fim de evitar
items.example: We left earlier in order to avoid the rush-hour traffic.
items.note: Follow in order to with the base verb, not an -ing form.

items.pt: então; por isso; de modo que
items.example: The printer was out of paper, so I used the one upstairs.
items.note: A common spoken-English coordinator linking a cause to its result.

items.example: The figures were incorrect. Therefore, we had to repeat the calculation.
items.note: A result connector, more formal than so; punctuation is often needed.

items.example: The roads were flooded. As a result, the bus service stopped.
items.note: Introduces a consequence of an earlier situation; generally more formal than so.

items.example: I am not sure whether the shop is open on Sundays.
items.note: Introduces uncertainty about a possibility; often interchangeable with if in this use.

items.example: I do not know if they have received my message.
items.note: Can introduce an indirect yes/no question after verbs such as know; not a condition here.

items.example: We are not sure whether the train will arrive on time.
items.note: A frequent construction for expressing uncertainty, followed by a clause.

items.example: Unless we leave soon, we will miss the beginning of the concert.
items.note: Introduces a negative condition: unless means if ... not; do not add another not unnecessarily.

items.example: Save the document now; otherwise, you might lose your changes.
items.note: Introduces the unwanted result if the previous instruction or condition is not met.

items.example: You may use my bicycle as long as you return it tonight.
items.note: Expresses a necessary condition; in future situations, a present verb commonly follows.

items.example: Take a jacket in case the evening becomes cold.
items.note: Explains a precaution taken now because something might happen later; different from if.

items.pt: caso chova; para o caso de chover
items.example: We always pack an umbrella in case it rains during the walk.
items.note: A concrete example of in case + present simple referring to a future possibility.

items.pt: a menos que haja um problema; salvo se houver problema
items.example: I will not interrupt you unless there’s a problem.
items.note: A practical negative condition used in the communication exercise.

sectionsChecked: A: Reason connectors because, as, since, so, the reason ... was that, because of and due to
B: Purpose with so (that), (in order) to and the purpose of
C: Results using so, therefore and as a result, including formality
D: Uncertainty and conditional logic with whether, unless, otherwise, as long as and in case
Exercises 94.1–94.4: because of transformations, connectors, workplace memo and personalised responses
